payload.answer: [hard] Never weaken a gate to reach the number: no pragma, omit, exclude, or include narrowing. If a line is genuinely unreachable, delete it rather than exempt it. [hard] Existing CI job and step names must stay byte-identical because branch protections match on them; the total-coverage gate is an additional step. [hard] Postgres integration tests stay real and are never mocked; PostgreSQL only, never SQLite. [hard] domain/ stays pure stdlib, enforced by import-linter. [hard] Conventional Commits; work on a feature branch off develop and open a PR into develop; never commit to main. [soft] tui/dashboard.py is Textual-based -- prefer Textual's own test harness (run_test/Pilot) over mocking the framework, since mocking a TUI framework tends to test the mock. [soft] Prefer a small number of focused tests per uncovered branch over one large test that sweeps many.

A coverage floor that silently excludes part of the tree is worse than no floor, because it reports green while real code goes unchecked. The four existing gates were added per layer and nothing ever covered what fell between them, so this gap has been invisible since tui/ was created. The total gate is the part that matters most: it makes the property self-maintaining, so a new top-level module cannot be added outside a floor by accident. Without it, closing today's gap just resets the same clock.

1) coverage report --include='src/vibey/*' --fail-under=100 passes on a single instrumented run of the full suite. 2) A NEW CI step enforces that total, and the four existing per-layer steps keep their exact current names. 3) Zero new coverage suppressions: no '# pragma: no cover', no omit= entries, no new exclude_lines, no narrowing of any --include. A reviewer must be able to diff the coverage config and see nothing weakened. 4) The new tests are real behavioural tests that would fail if the behaviour broke -- not calls that merely execute lines for the counter. 5) All seven existing gates still pass: ruff check, ruff format --check, mypy --strict, the four per-layer floors, import-linter, bandit, pip-audit.

Bring every line and branch under src/vibey to 100% branch coverage, and add a CI gate that covers ALL of src/vibey so no module can sit outside a floor again. Today four per-layer gates cover domain/, application/, infrastructure/ and cli/ and all four pass at 100%. Two modules sit outside every one of them and are therefore invisible to CI: src/vibey/tui/dashboard.py at 84% (23 uncovered statements, 15 partial branches) and src/vibey/bootstrap.py at 98% (2 statements, 2 partial branches, lines 279 and 501). The real total is 99%, not 100%. Close both gaps with genuine tests, then add a fifth gate: coverage report --include='src/vibey/*' --fail-under=100.

payload.answer: Architectural hygiene immediately before the codebase grows. Runbooks 16-21 add an operator, a shared-library extraction, two new products and several new modules, and every one of them is a chance to land outside the floors. Closing the gap after that expansion is strictly more work than closing it now. There is also a live example of why uncovered code hides defects: `vibey cost` reads its caps from config['budget']['max_dollars_per_cycle'], a key nothing writes, so it silently displays hardcoded $40/$250 defaults instead of the project's real configured cap. Fixing that is OUT OF SCOPE here -- it is named only as evidence that unexercised code drifts.

Developers adding a new top-level module, and PR reviewers. The failure this prevents is specific: someone creates src/vibey/<newthing>/ and it lands outside all four per-layer gates, so CI reports 100% while the module is untested. That already happened once -- it is how tui/ reached 84% unnoticed. Reviewers benefit because 'coverage is green' becomes a statement about the whole tree instead of four subdirectories of it.

Concretely, from the current report. bootstrap.py line 279: the branch where a project configures max_cycle_turns but NOT max_cycle_dollars (and the neither-configured case) -- the budget brake's construction predicate. bootstrap.py line 501: the asyncpg pool returning None, which is the guard before 'did not create a pool'. tui/dashboard.py line 87: fetch_dashboard_state against an unknown project id, which raises ValueError. Lines 99-108: the ledger-scan branches for every phase-decision event kind -- VISUAL_DESIGN opted_in/declined/accepted/waived and DEPLOYMENT opted_in/declined -- each of which sets a different banner value and none of which any current test produces. Line 114: a project whose managed worktree root does not exist yet, versus one with worktrees present. The remaining partial branches around lines 278-295, 342-348 and 422-465 are render and refresh paths: empty circuits, empty queue, and the exit arms of loops that today only ever run with data. Prefer driving these through Textual's own Pilot harness so they exercise real rendering rather than a mock of it.

payload.answer: Making every path intentional, with a second-order property that matters more here: the total gate is SELF-MAINTAINING. Four per-layer gates depend on somebody remembering to add a fifth when they create a new top-level package. --include='src/vibey/*' removes that dependency on memory, which is the actual defect being fixed -- the current 84% in tui/ is not a testing failure, it is a gate-topology failure. The zero-exemptions rule carries the corollary that dead code becomes visible: if a line genuinely cannot be reached, the honest resolution is to delete it, and a pragma would hide exactly the signal worth having.

Integrated into the existing files, matching the current layout. tests/tui/test_dashboard.py and tests/test_bootstrap.py both already exist, so the new tests belong beside their neighbours rather than in a parallel structure. A dedicated 'coverage gap' suite is the wrong shape twice over: it decays into a junk drawer nobody maintains, and its very name announces that the tests were written for the counter rather than for the behaviour, which invites exactly the line-touching non-tests the acceptance criteria forbid.

It depends on which kind of issue, and the distinction is important. If covering a branch shows the branch is UNREACHABLE, deleting it is the fix, not a refactor -- that is the zero-exemptions rule working as intended, and covering it is impossible by definition. If the code is merely awkward -- an overcomplicated conditional that is reachable and correct -- cover the design as it stands and raise the refactor as a separate item. Refactoring under a coverage mandate is how a coverage task quietly becomes an unreviewed redesign, and it makes the diff impossible to review against its stated purpose. The one thing never acceptable is changing production behaviour to make a test easier to write.

Keep all five. The per-layer gates are not made redundant by the total -- they carry ATTRIBUTION. A failing total gate says 'something regressed'; a failing 'Gate 4c - pytest infrastructure layer' says which layer, which is what makes the failure actionable at a glance. There is also a hard mechanical reason: the existing CI step names are matched by branch protection rules, so removing or renaming them breaks merge requirements. The total gate is an additional step, never a replacement.

payload.answer: All four combinations, because line 279 is an OR over two isinstance checks and each arm needs both outcomes: {max_cycle_turns: 10} alone, {max_cycle_dollars: 50.0} alone, both together, and neither (budget_source stays None). Add a fifth that is not a combination but the reason the isinstance guards exist at all: a config carrying a NON-NUMERIC value, e.g. {max_cycle_dollars: '50'} as a string or None. That must be treated as absent rather than crashing or silently coercing -- a project whose cap is a string must not end up with no brake while appearing to have one. That case is the one most likely to occur in real life, via hand-edited config or a bad import.

One focused test per decision kind -- six tests: VISUAL_DESIGN opted_in / declined / accepted / waived, and DEPLOYMENT opted_in / declined. Each builds the minimal ledger that reaches that state and asserts the resulting banner value. Composite scenarios are the wrong shape here: the branches are a single elif chain, so a composite test passes as long as ANY arm fires and tells you nothing about which. Add one seventh test for the chain's implicit else -- a ledger containing only unrelated event kinds, where both banners must stay None. That arm has no elif of its own, which is exactly why it is easy to leave uncovered.

Three project states plus one error case. (1) Brand new project: no jobs ever queued, no engine_health rows, no worktree directory -- exercises empty queue_depth, empty circuits, and the managed_root.exists() false arm at line 114. (2) Active project with jobs and recorded circuits but no worktree directory on disk -- separates 'no worktrees' from 'new project', which the first case conflates. (3) Project with a populated worktree root, covering the iterdir/sorted arm. (4) fetch_dashboard_state against an unknown project id, asserting ValueError -- line 87. Drive rendering through Textual's Pilot harness rather than asserting on widget internals, so the tests survive a layout change.

bootstrap.py line 501: asyncpg.create_pool returning None, guarding the 'asyncpg did not create a pool' RuntimeError. Test it by monkeypatching asyncpg.create_pool to return None and asserting build_app raises that RuntimeError with that message. It is a real defensive branch -- create_pool is typed as returning Pool | None -- so it cannot be deleted as unreachable, and a mock is legitimate here precisely because the condition cannot be produced by a healthy database. Keep the assertion on the message, not just the type: the message is the only thing that tells an operator what failed.
